items.title: Desktop: multi-minute idle gaps and missing final delivery after tool output is confirmed

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
Environment
- macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon arm64
- Desktop app 26.1013.40934 (build 20770)
- Model gpt-6.1-sol; reasoning high and service tier priority at the time of the incident

Problem
Repeated multi-minute gaps between useful actions, plus no final response after an external tool has already produced the requested artifact. This has blocked normal local project work across October 19–21, 2026.

Observed timeline (Asia/Taipei, UTC+8, October 21)
1. At 10:57 a local task was asked to regenerate an expired preview QR code.
2. The first external developer-tool invocation reported compile_start / Timeout (code 10). This external timeout is a separate problem and should not be conflated with Codex latency.
3. A Codex tool result returned at 10:58:49. The next tool invocation was at 11:09:03, roughly 10 minutes later. The cause of the interval is unknown.
4. After retrying, the new QR image had a modification time of 11:12.
5. At 11:17:37 a Codex tool output explicitly confirmed that the artifact existed. Codex did not subsequently deliver the result before the turn was interrupted at 11:21:56.
6. Another turn started at 11:30:52. At 11:37:58 there were still no new assistant messages or tool invocations in the local transcript.

Other observations
- Similar 14–26 minute intervals occurred on October 19. Some involved image generation; the reason for other gaps is unconfirmed.
- Desktop logs included websocket_reconnect_recovery_start and Local Work executor read_error / websocket_error / timed_out. These are leads only; they are not confirmed causes of the local Codex pauses.
- The affected conversation spans several days. Its on-disk JSONL is about 2.53 GB with many embedded images. This is on-disk size, not the active model context size. The performance impact is unconfirmed.
- Default reasoning was later changed to medium as a mitigation; improvement has not been verified.

Expected
When an external tool fails, report the specific error promptly or retry within a bounded workflow. When the requested artifact is successfully created and confirmed, return it promptly. Do not remain active for multiple minutes without useful progress or final delivery.

Requested investigation
Please distinguish inference/queue latency, turn scheduling or recovery, tool completion to final-answer latency, and long-history loading/compaction. Private chat IDs and redacted log excerpts can be provided through a private support channel if required. No credentials, project source code, personal email, local filesystem paths, or private chat IDs are included in this public report.

这些报告未描述“一个窗口卡死且系统控件消失、另一个窗口正常、Dock 激活优先落到故障窗口”的完整组合，因此单独记录这一窗口症状；是否存在共同根因仍需维护者确认。

同一使用过程中还遇到频繁意外重启，有时任务会自动恢复；这一重启现象会在 #43180 下另行补充。目前未确认两种现象是否相关。

应用版本已通过本机 Info.plist 核实。本次未取得与该窗口症状对应的崩溃堆栈。现有截图只包含侧栏，没有呈现完整标题栏或两个窗口，故未将其作为此现象的复现证据上传。

items.title: MultiAgentV2 eviction lacks a live-background-command guard; safe completed-child release needed

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app

labels.name: subagent

items.body:
## What version of the Codex App are you using?

26.1013.40934, build 20770; embedded `codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2`.

## What subscription do you have?

Account tier was not recorded in the diagnostic package. The isolated reproduction below uses an unauthenticated local model stub and does not require a subscription or API key.

## Scope and related reports

This report focuses on **safe runtime reclamation for completed V2 subagents, specifically the missing live-background-command guard in eviction**. It includes a runnable isolated test showing why explicit archive is not a safe conditional-cleanup substitute, and a proposed maintainer regression test for the background-command risk.

Existing retention reports: [#38247](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/38247) and [#55141](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55141). This is not intended as another generic MCP-memory report: the additional finding is the background-process eligibility gap and the safety contract needed before making completed-child reclamation automatic. [#36095](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/36095) describes a related but different concurrent-follow-up/residency-accounting race.

**Evidence boundary:** active-thread archive behavior was reproduced; background-command termination through V2 eviction is a source-supported risk and has not yet been reproduced at runtime. No loss of a user's background command is claimed.

## Summary

Completed V2 subagents can retain their runtimes and associated MCP processes after reporting their final result. The existing idle-unload timer only helps after the final subscription is removed; completion alone does not reliably establish that condition.

Please provide a lifecycle operation that releases an eligible completed subagent's runtime without interrupting active work, background commands, its parent, or siblings, and without changing archive state or losing persisted results.

Two findings make an external cleanup workaround unsafe:

1. **Runtime-reproduced:** `thread/archive` accepts a currently active thread and unloads it. Thus `read status -> if idle, archive` has a time-of-check/time-of-use race. Explicit archive may intentionally cancel work; this report does **not** claim that explicit archive must change semantics. It demonstrates why archive is not a substitute for conditional idle release.
2. **Source-confirmed risk, not a runtime reproduction of background-command loss:** the internal V2 eviction guard does not check live background terminals. Successful eviction shuts down the session, whose shutdown path terminates all unified-exec processes. If a child has completed its model turn while a yielded background command is still running, that command appears vulnerable to termination on eviction.

## Environment

- Observed and retested: 2026-10-21.
- MacBook Air, Apple Silicon / arm64, 24 GiB RAM.
- macOS 27.0.1, build 26A434.
- Desktop bundle: version 26.1013.40934, build 20770.
- Embedded executable: `codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2`.
- Source checkout inspected: `openai/codex`, commit `4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4`.
- V2 collaboration tools available in the affected session: spawn, follow-up, interrupt, send, list, wait; no callable V2 `close_agent` or conditional unload operation was exposed.

## Impact and scope of observations

During prolonged parallel use, the machine accumulated several hundred Node/tool processes and severe memory pressure. This is a system-wide operational observation, not a controlled per-agent memory benchmark, and not a claim that every process was orphaned. Many retained tool processes still had a live app-server parent and pipes.

Completed subagent runtimes remained loaded despite final results being available. Manually unloading individually verified completed runtimes released their associated tool processes. This motivated the request for safe automatic release, rather than a PID-age or process-name killer.

The exact reason every retained child remains resident is not established by the minimal test below. Completion notification, subscription lifetime and V2 residency need investigation together. Do not infer that a completed turn means a task has no remaining background work.

## Reproduction A: archive is not a conditional idle-release operation

`repro_archive_active.py` is embedded in full below (Python standard library only).

Run against the affected executable:

```sh
python3 repro_archive_active.py \
  --codex-bin /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex-cli/CodexCLI.app/Contents/MacOS/codex \
  --output archive-result.json
```

For another installation, replace `--codex-bin` with its executable path. If `codex` is already on PATH, the argument can be omitted.

The script:

1. Creates a temporary, isolated `CODEX_HOME` and working directory. It does not connect to the Desktop app-server, copy credentials, or use any existing chat ID.
2. Starts its own stdio app-server and a loopback HTTP server implementing a minimal Responses stream. No real model inference is requested.
3. Initializes the protocol, starts a synthetic thread and starts one turn.
4. Keeps the local response stream open and verifies `thread/read` returns `status.type = active`.
5. Calls `thread/archive` on **only that synthetic thread** and then `thread/loaded/list`.
6. Stops its own app-server and HTTP server and removes its temporary state.

The relevant protocol sequence is:

```text
initialize -> initialized
thread/start -> synthetic thread ID
turn/start -> local response stream held open
thread/read -> { "status": { "type": "active", "activeFlags": [] } }
thread/archive -> { "result": {} }
thread/loaded/list -> synthetic thread ID absent
```

Observed again with the script embedded below:

```json
{
  "before_archive_status": {"type": "active", "activeFlags": []},
  "archive_response": {"id": 5, "result": {}},
  "still_loaded_after_archive": false,
  "active_archive_observed": true,
  "real_model_inference_used": false,
  "isolated_app_server_exited": true
}
```

The full sanitized result is in `archive-result.json`. A future rejection or changed behavior is reported by `active_archive_observed: false`; a failed precondition raises an error. Do not use this test to archive a real user thread.

## Reproduction B: maintainer regression test for background commands

**Proposed integration test; not executed in this report.** This case requires access to the internal V2 eviction primitive or a controlled V2 capacity-eviction harness.

1. Create a V2 parent and child with an isolated MCP test server.
2. In the child, start an owned unified-exec command that yields a session ID and continues updating a temporary heartbeat file. Keep the command alive with an explicit test-controlled release condition.
3. Complete the child's model turn while that command remains running. Assert the child is `Completed`, has no active model turn, and its background terminal is still live.
4. Invoke the normal internal conditional-eviction path. For a black-box variant, create sufficient additional children to trigger residency pressure and confirm this child is the selected candidate.
5. Assert that eviction returns `Busy` or an equivalent structured reason and the heartbeat/process remains alive. Also assert that the parent, siblings and their MCP processes remain unaffected.
6. Finish the command, retry eviction, and assert that only this child's runtime and owned MCP process are released, with its final result/history preserved.

The inspected implementation appears to admit the child in step 4 and terminate its background process during shutdown. This predicted result still needs the runtime integration test above; no claim is made that a user's background command was actually lost during this investigation.

## Source evidence

All links are pinned to the inspected commit, rather than a moving branch.

- [`try_evict_v2_thread`, residency gate and exact runtime identity](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/residency.rs#L35-L95): uses the residency write gate and keeps it through shutdown/persistence/removal. This is a useful basis for a safe operation.
- [`is_unloadable`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/residency.rs#L313-L327): checks terminal-like agent status, no active turn, no outstanding durable sleep and no trigger-turn mailbox items. There is no background-terminal check here.
- [`shutdown_session_runtime`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/session/handlers.rs#L290-L330): calls `unified_exec_manager.terminate_all_processes()` and shuts down the MCP runtime.
- [Archive preparation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L1062-L1094) removes/shuts down the runtime without a conditional idle guard. [Archive implementation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L1714-L1805) operates on the spawned subtree. The list-state permit does not provide the required turn-admission guard.
- [Delayed unloading](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_lifecycle.rs#L400-L465) uses the V2 eviction primitive and retries `Busy`; it depends on subscription release.
- [Completion routing](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/completion.rs) delivers terminal outcomes to the parent, but does not itself provide a public completed-child release operation.

## Existing mitigation and its limits

Setting `thread_unload_delay_secs = 300` was tested with the installed binary using two isolated synthetic threads, each with its own small MCP test process. After unsubscribing one thread, it and its MCP process remained present at 295 seconds and were gone at 302 seconds. The subscribed control and its MCP process survived. All test processes were subsequently cleaned up.

This verifies the post-unsubscribe delay, not automatic release of retained child subscriptions, background-command safety, or history restoration. Lowering this value alone does not address the reported lifecycle gap.

## Requested behavior and acceptance criteria

Provide automatic completed-child release and/or an explicit conditional release operation available to the owning parent/controller. A proposed name such as `thread/releaseIfIdle` is illustrative; it is not an existing API.

1. Trigger a release attempt after a child completes, with a documented retention/grace policy. Do not rely only on last-subscriber removal or later capacity pressure. Completion must not itself be treated as sufficient proof of eligibility.
2. Under the same admission/residency synchronization used by turn starts and message delivery, verify the exact current runtime generation and that there are no active or queued turns, pending approval/input waits, durable sleeps, trigger messages, live background commands, or active dependent descendants. Unknown state must fail closed.
3. Coordinate background-process creation and completion with that synchronization. Listing processes first and shutting down later is insufficient.
4. Return a structured `Busy` reason with no shutdown side effects when ineligible. A concurrent follow-up must either prevent eviction or be delivered safely after rehydration; it must never be interrupted or dropped by cleanup.
5. Persist the terminal result, relevant mailbox state and history before releasing resources. Do not change archive state or cascade shutdown into parents/siblings. Active descendants must prevent release unless ownership can be preserved explicitly.
6. Release only resources owned by the selected runtime, including its MCP processes. Shared runtimes/resources need ownership/refcount handling rather than broad termination.
7. Preserve the ability to resume the child from persisted state with an explicit contract for which volatile tool state is not retained.
8. Cover races, cancellation and partial shutdown/persistence failures with tests. A stale completion event must not evict a newer runtime registered under the same thread ID. Include the background-command regression above, active siblings/parent, pending approval/input, durable sleep, queued follow-up, history read/resume, and process-leak checks.

## Embedded files and disclosure

- `repro_archive_active.py`: locally retested reproducer.
- `archive-result.json`: fresh synthetic result, without real thread IDs or local account paths.
- `verification-summary.json`: sanitized summary of the separate five-minute test and source-evidence status.

No production logs, credentials, real conversation contents or user process listings are included. The reproducer and sanitized results are embedded below so the report is self-contained.

<details>
<summary>repro_archive_active.py</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Probe archive semantics using an isolated Codex app-server and local fake model.

No production CODEX_HOME, chat IDs, credentials, or real inference are used.
The test archives ONLY the synthetic thread created by this script.
"""

import argparse
import http.server
import json
import os
import queue
import shutil
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading
import time
from pathlib import Path


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--codex-bin", default=shutil.which("codex"))
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not args.codex_bin:
        parser.error("Pass --codex-bin pointing to the Codex executable under test")
    binary = str(Path(args.codex_bin).resolve())
    version = subprocess.check_output([binary, "--version"], text=True).strip()
    ready = threading.Event()
    stop = threading.Event()

    class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self, *unused: object) -> None:
            pass

        def do_POST(self) -> None:
            self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0)))
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
            self.end_headers()
            event = {
                "type": "response.created",
                "response": {
                    "id": "resp_local_probe",
                    "object": "response",
                    "created_at": int(time.time()),
                    "model": "probe",
                    "status": "in_progress",
                    "output": [],
                },
            }
            self.wfile.write(("data: " + json.dumps(event) + "\n\n").encode())
            self.wfile.flush()
            ready.set()
            stop.wait(90)

    server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
    server.daemon_threads = True
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    process = None
    result = None
    try:
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="codex-archive-repro-") as temporary:
            root = Path(temporary)
            home = root / "codex-home"
            home.mkdir()
            (home / "config.toml").write_text(
                'model = "probe"\nmodel_provider = "probe"\n'
                'approval_policy = "never"\nsandbox_mode = "read-only"\n'
                '[model_providers.probe]\nname = "Local lifecycle test"\n'
                f'base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/v1"\n'
                'wire_api = "responses"\nrequires_openai_auth = false\n',
                encoding="utf-8",
            )
            environment = {
                key: os.environ[key]
                for key in ("PATH", "HOME", "TMPDIR", "LANG", "SYSTEMROOT")
                if key in os.environ
            }
            environment["CODEX_HOME"] = str(home)
            messages = queue.Queue()
            with (root / "app-server.log").open("w") as log:
                process = subprocess.Popen(
                    [binary, "app-server"],
                    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                    stderr=log,
                    text=True,
                    cwd=root,
                    env=environment,
                )

                def reader() -> None:
                    try:
                        for line in process.stdout:
                            messages.put(json.loads(line))
                    finally:
                        messages.put(None)

                threading.Thread(target=reader, daemon=True).start()
                serial = 0

                def rpc(method: str, params: dict) -> dict:
                    nonlocal serial
                    serial += 1
                    process.stdin.write(
                        json.dumps(
                            {
                                "id": serial,
                                "method": method,
                                "params": params,
                            }
                        )
                        + "\n"
                    )
                    process.stdin.flush()
                    deadline = time.monotonic() + 30
                    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
                        message = messages.get(
                            timeout=max(0.1, deadline - time.monotonic())
                        )
                        if message is None:
                            raise RuntimeError("app-server exited before replying")
                        if message.get("id") == serial:
                            return message
                    raise TimeoutError(method)

                def request(method: str, params: dict) -> dict:
                    response = rpc(method, params)
                    if "error" in response:
                        raise RuntimeError(f"{method}: {response['error']}")
                    return response["result"]

                try:
                    request(
                        "initialize",
                        {
                            "clientInfo": {
                                "name": "archive_safety_probe",
                                "version": "1",
                            },
                            "capabilities": {"experimentalApi": True},
                        },
                    )
                    process.stdin.write('{"method":"initialized","params":{}}\n')
                    process.stdin.flush()
                    thread_id = request(
                        "thread/start",
                        {
                            "cwd": str(root),
                            "baseInstructions": "Local synthetic test only.",
                        },
                    )["thread"]["id"]
                    request(
                        "turn/start",
                        {
                            "threadId": thread_id,
                            "input": [{"type": "text", "text": "Local lifecycle test"}],
                        },
                    )
                    if not ready.wait(20):
                        raise RuntimeError("Local fake model stream was not reached")
                    before = request(
                        "thread/read",
                        {
                            "threadId": thread_id,
                            "includeTurns": True,
                        },
                    )["thread"]["status"]
                    if before.get("type") != "active":
                        raise RuntimeError(f"Precondition failed: {before}")
                    archive = rpc("thread/archive", {"threadId": thread_id})
                    loaded = thread_id in request("thread/loaded/list", {})["data"]
                    result = {
                        "codex_version": version,
                        "before_archive_status": before,
                        "archive_response": archive,
                        "still_loaded_after_archive": loaded,
                        "active_archive_observed": "result" in archive and not loaded,
                        "real_model_inference_used": False,
                    }
                finally:
                    stop.set()
                    process.stdin.close()
                    try:
                        process.wait(timeout=5)
                    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                        process.terminate()
                        try:
                            process.wait(timeout=5)
                        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                            process.kill()
                            process.wait(timeout=5)
                    if result is not None:
                        result["isolated_app_server_exited"] = (
                            process.poll() is not None
                        )
    finally:
        stop.set()
        server.shutdown()
        server.server_close()
    rendered = json.dumps(result, indent=2)
    print(rendered)
    if args.output:
        args.output.write_text(rendered + "\n", encoding="utf-8")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

</details>

  },

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

### Use case

I'm trying to connect MCP servers that require non-bearer HTTP headers (e.g. X-MCP-Lockdown: true). For clients like claude code, I can do this via:

`claude mcp add my-server --transport http --header "X-MCP-Lockdown: true" https://example.com/mcp`

For Codex, `codex mcp add `has no --header flag. The only way to set static headers today is by manually editing ~/.codex/config.toml via `http_headers` — which was added in #5241. This makes it impossible to construct a fully self-contained setup command for servers that require non-bearer headers.

### Suggestion
Add a `--header "Name: Value"` flag (repeatable) to codex mcp add, analogous to claude code's implementation. Example:


```
codex mcp add my-server \
  --url https://example.com/mcp \
  --header "X-MCP-Lockdown: true"
```


This would write the values into `http_headers` in `config.toml`, just as `--bearer-token-env-var` writes into `bearer_token_env_var`.

#### Affected servers

Servers that currently can't be fully configured via CLI due to required non-bearer headers include github-mcp-server (X-MCP-Lockdown) and others.

The -`-header` flag could be added at line 352 of `codex-rs/cli/src/mcp_cmd.rs`, alongside the existing `--bearer-token-env-var` argument, and the parsed values written into the `http_headers` map in the server config — the same field added in #5241.

### Additional information

_No response_

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.4894.0 (Windows package: OpenAI.Codex; Fedora app version not recorded)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Fedora Linux (RPM desktop app); also tested from the web interface. Current successful retry: Chrome on Windows 11. Exact OS build/kernel not recorded.

### What issue are you seeing?

Browser access has been inconsistent across Work sessions. The Browser extension was installed and connected, and selected-tab information could reach the assistant, but some sessions could not use the browser controls.

Observed on 20–21 October 2026:
- Some sessions displayed "Some tools are temporarily not available".
- The assistant reported that Browser instructions and selected-tab metadata were present, but the browser-control tool was not available. Asking it to open x.com produced no navigation.
- An execution attempt in an affected session returned: "No usable execution environment is available. Wait for an environment to become available before using this tool."
- In a separate in-app browser session, the assistant reported "Tab not found in browser 1". It appeared to access separate signed-out tabs rather than the signed-in tabs visible in the chat.
- Manual takeover in that in-app browser session displayed "Cloud browser is not available".

These are observations from different attempts; I cannot establish whether they share one root cause.

Important update: on 21 October, the connected Chrome Browser tool works in this web session. The assistant successfully read and claimed this GitHub issue tab and filled this form. This demonstrates inconsistent behavior across sessions/environments rather than a complete, permanent failure.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Feedback ID: 6275df0b-483f-4e78-af89-e4e3529bbd8a

### What is the expected behavior?

When a browser is connected and available to a Work session, the assistant should receive working browser controls and act on the requested tab in that browser.

For the in-app browser, the controlled tabs should match the tabs shown to the user, including their current session state.

If the environment or browser is unavailable, the UI and assistant should clearly identify the unavailable component and provide a consistent, actionable error.

### Additional information

### Steps to reproduce

Feedback ID: 6275df0b-483f-4e78-af89-e4e3529bbd8a

Reproduction used in affected sessions:
1. Open a Work chat with the Browser plugin enabled and the browser extension connected.
2. Keep a normal website open in the connected browser.
3. Ask: "Use the Browser plugin and open x.com."
4. Observe that the assistant cannot navigate because browser controls are unavailable, even though selected-tab details may be visible.
5. Start another Work chat and retry. Results have varied across sessions.

Separate in-app browser attempt:
1. Open signed-in LinkedIn/X pages in ChatGPT's in-app browser.
2. Ask the assistant to interact with the visible page.
3. Observe a tab lookup failure or access to different signed-out tabs.
4. Try manual takeover; "Cloud browser is not available" was displayed.

The original missing-tool failure was observed on 20 October 2026 at approximately 9:08 PM Saudi Arabia time (UTC+3). Further failures were observed on 21 October before the successful external Chrome retry.

Token-limit and context-window usage were not recorded. The issue also occurred in newly started chats.

### Troubleshooting and context

Troubleshooting and reporting already performed:
- Updated the Fedora RPM desktop app to the latest available version.
- Retried from the browser interface.
- Started multiple new chats and retried with Astra and Sol 6.1.
- Submitted feedback from several affected chats and supplied their chat IDs to OpenAI support.

## Summary
An existing Dot has disappeared from the macOS ChatGPT desktop sidebar, while the same user's Dot remains accessible and replies normally at https://chatgpt.com/dots/home in Chrome. The desktop screenshot is already in the ChatGPT view, so this is not explained by being in the Codex view.

Please investigate desktop Dot navigation/configuration loading and provide a supported recovery path that preserves existing conversations, local tasks and computer authorization.

## Environment
- ChatGPT desktop production version 26.1016.51333, build 21161 (verified from installed app metadata).
- Built-in updater reports `up_to_date`.
- macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple Silicon arm64.
- Observed October 21, 2026, approximately 13:00–13:15 UTC+7.

## Observed behavior
1. Desktop app runs and existing Work/Codex tasks remain listed.
2. ChatGPT sidebar shows New chat and pinned conversations, but no Dot entry.
3. Chrome at /dots/home still shows the existing Dot, its conversation and working replies (user-provided screenshot).
4. The app log recorded successful Dot room/history fetches around 06:00 UTC, followed by these warnings:

```
2026-10-21T06:00:48.620Z warning [electron-message-handler] Orbit catalog task metadata could not be loaded ... status=undefined
2026-10-21T06:03:52.526Z warning [electron-message-handler] Orbit catalog task metadata could not be loaded ... status=undefined
```

The warnings are correlation only, not an established root cause. A targeted check of the currently running main-process logs did NOT find `Workspace routing is unavailable`, status 432, or `/tbo/primary` 404. This distinguishes the captured evidence from some related reports; it does not rule out uncaptured configuration failures.

## Expected
An accessible existing Dot should remain reachable in desktop navigation. If availability or navigation metadata cannot load, surface a recoverable error rather than silently hiding the entry.

## Checks and limits
- Confirmed app process is running and built-in updater reports current.
- No logout, reset, cache deletion, reinstall, settings change or forced process termination performed, to preserve ongoing tasks.
- No deterministic fresh-account reproduction; this report describes the affected user's observed state.
- No claim that the Dot was deleted or that account entitlement was revoked.
- Screenshots and full logs are intentionally omitted because they contain private conversations. No account/workspace IDs, credentials or private message contents are included.

## Related reports
- #50283 (macOS missing Dot; reported routing errors differ from evidence captured here)
- #51213 (desktop entry disappears while background tasks continue)

Submitted with AI assistance at the affected user's explicit request.

items.body:
## Summary

On ChatGPT Windows Desktop, a fresh **non-Project** chat can ignore an explicitly selected **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** configuration on the **very first request**.

The first response is already attributed to **6 Thinking**, and the composer shows **Medium** afterward.

This differs from a later automatic model switch: in the affected Windows Desktop chat, the manually selected GPT-5.6 Sol / High configuration is never used at all.

A control test on ChatGPT Web with the same account and the same non-Project setup behaves correctly: the first response uses **5.6 Sol** and **High remains selected**.

> Disclosure: The reproduction tests and screenshots were performed/provided by the user. This issue was drafted and submitted by ChatGPT at the user's explicit request based on those tests and observations.

## Environment

- ChatGPT Windows Desktop
- Version: **26.1016.51333**
- Release date shown in About: **October 21, 2026**
- Windows
- Reproduced on October 21, 2026
- Fresh **non-Project** chat

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open ChatGPT Windows Desktop.
2. Start a fresh chat **outside any Project**.
3. Before sending the first message, select **GPT-5.6 Sol** with **High** reasoning.
4. Send the first message.
5. Check the first response's per-message model attribution.
6. Observe that the first response is attributed to **6 Thinking**.
7. Observe that the composer/reasoning control shows **Medium**.

## Actual behavior

The explicit model/reasoning selection is ignored on the first request:

`GPT-5.6 Sol / High selected`
→ first request is sent
→ first response is attributed to `6 Thinking`
→ composer shows `Medium`

So this is not only a stale picker label. The first response is actually generated by a different model family than the one explicitly selected.

## Expected behavior

A fresh non-Project chat should use the explicitly selected **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** configuration for the first request and keep it active until the user changes it.

## Control test: ChatGPT Web

Using the same account and the same non-Project setup on ChatGPT Web:

1. Start a fresh non-Project chat.
2. Select **GPT-5.6 Sol / High**.
3. Send the first message.
4. The first response is attributed to **5.6 Sol**.
5. **High remains selected** afterward.

This makes the Windows Desktop first-turn behavior look client-specific rather than an account-level or model-availability issue.

## Evidence

A screenshot captured by the user shows, in the same fresh non-Project Windows Desktop chat:

- the first response identifying GPT-6,
- per-message attribution showing **6 Thinking**,
- the composer showing **Medium**.

A corresponding ChatGPT Web control test shows **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** working normally.

The screenshots can be attached separately if needed.

## Related issues

- #54618 — **Codex Windows app automatically switches manually selected model from GPT-5.6 Luna to GPT-6 Astra Light**
  - Related because both involve a manually selected model being replaced on Windows.
  - Distinct here because this reproduces on the **very first request of a fresh non-Project Chat**, and the selected GPT-5.6 configuration is never used at all.
- #55777 — **[ChatGPT Projects] GPT-5.6 Sol / High switches to GPT-6 Thinking after the first turn**
  - Related but a different lifecycle boundary.
  - #55777 is Project-specific: its first request correctly uses GPT-5.6 Sol, then the conversation changes after the first response.
  - This issue is non-Project and fails **before/at first-turn dispatch**.
- #47710 — **Model selection reverts to gpt-6-astra in every new remote chat**
  - Similar new-chat model reconciliation behavior, but it concerns remote chats and reverts before sending.

## Why this appears distinct from #54618

#54618 reports that the Windows app automatically changes a manually selected GPT-5.6 model to a GPT-6 model.

This reproduction narrows the failure to a specific lifecycle point:

- fresh **non-Project** Chat,
- explicit **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** selection before any message,
- **first response already uses GPT-6 Thinking**,
- same account and setup works correctly on ChatGPT Web.

That suggests a Windows Desktop new-chat initialization / first-request dispatch problem rather than only a later model-selection persistence issue.

macOS 26.3, arm64.

### What issue are you seeing?

I have 15 Codex chats with stale worktree attachments. The referenced worktree folders no longer exist, but their attachment records remain.

All affected chats are based in an existing main repository checkout. Only their attached worktree paths are missing.

Anonymized example:
- Chat working directory: `/Users/<user>/dev/<repo>`
- Missing attached worktree: `/Users/<user>/.codex/worktrees/<old-worktree>/<repo>`

These missing paths are on the internal drive, not an external volume that is temporarily disconnected.

Codex provides an “Archive worktree” action, but read-only inspection of the installed app suggests that it tries to read the checkout to prepare recovery information before removing the attachment. That appears to prevent cleanup when the folder is already missing. We could not find an exposed action specifically for detaching a missing worktree.

**Verification limit:** The stale attachments and missing directories were verified. The predicted archive failure is based on read-only implementation inspection; we have not attempted the archive action on these 15 attachments, and no runtime archive error is being claimed.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The exact historical removal sequence has not been reconstructed, so this is a report of a verified existing state rather than a fresh reproduction:

1. A Codex chat remains based in a valid main repository checkout.
2. The chat has a worktree attachment referring to a separate checkout.
3. That checkout directory is no longer present.
4. The stale worktree attachment remains, with no confirmed supported way to detach it while retaining the chat and history.

We left the attachments unchanged after the read-only investigation. We did not recreate dummy checkouts, edit the app database, or delete/archive the chats.

### What is the expected behavior?

Please add a supported “Remove stale attachment” or “Detach missing worktree” option that:

- Verifies that the referenced folder is missing and warns if an external drive may simply be disconnected.
- Removes only the stale worktree association.
- Preserves the chat, its complete history, working directory, branches, and unrelated attachments.
- Does not recreate the worktree or require a recovery snapshot.
- Supports reviewing and cleaning up multiple stale attachments together.

The action should clearly state that it removes an attachment only and does not delete the chat or any repository files.

Expected outcome: the 15 chats remain available with their full history and valid main-repository working directories, while the obsolete worktree attachments disappear.

### Additional information

Related: #51534 reports missing-worktree cleanup problems on Windows, including a runtime ownership error and watcher warnings. This report concerns macOS stale attachments and the need for safe detachment; we have not verified those Windows-specific symptoms here.

Usernames, private project names, chat titles, chat/session IDs, and raw logs are omitted. All example paths are placeholders.

items.title: [ChatGPT Projects] GPT-5.6 Sol / High switches to GPT-6 Thinking after the first turn

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
## Summary

When starting a new ChatGPT conversation **inside a Project**, an explicitly selected **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** configuration is honored for the first turn, but after the first response the conversation state changes without user action.

This is **not only a model-picker UI issue**. Per-message model attribution confirms that the effective model used for subsequent requests actually changes:

- First response: **5.6 Sol**
- Second response: **6 Thinking**

The reasoning selector also changes from **High** to **Medium** after the first response.

A control test on ChatGPT Web outside Projects keeps **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** stable.

> Disclosure: The reproduction tests and screenshots were performed/provided by the user. This issue was drafted and submitted by ChatGPT at the user's explicit request based on those tests and observations.

## Environment

- ChatGPT Web on Windows
- ChatGPT Windows Desktop
- Windows Desktop version: **26.1016.51333**
- Release date shown in About: **October 21, 2026**
- Reproduced on October 21, 2026

## Primary reproduction: ChatGPT Web + Project

1. Open an existing ChatGPT Project.
2. Start a new chat inside the Project.
3. Select **GPT-5.6 Sol** with **High** reasoning before sending the first message.
4. Send the first message.
5. Check the first response's per-message model attribution.
   - It shows **5.6 Sol**.
6. After the first response completes, check the reasoning selector.
   - It has changed from **High** to **Medium** without user action.
7. Do not manually change the selector.
8. Send a second message.
9. Check the second response's per-message attribution.
   - It now shows **6 Thinking**.

## Actual behavior

The first request correctly uses GPT-5.6 Sol.

After the first response, the Project conversation's model/reasoning state changes without user action:

`GPT-5.6 Sol / High`
→ first turn uses `5.6 Sol`
→ reasoning selector changes to `Medium`
→ next turn uses `6 Thinking`

The effective model therefore changes, not just the displayed selector.

## Expected behavior

The explicitly selected **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** configuration should remain active for subsequent turns until the user changes it manually.

Creating or hydrating a Project conversation should not overwrite the user's explicit model or reasoning selection.

## Control test: ChatGPT Web outside Projects

The same selection behaves normally outside Projects:

1. Start a normal non-Project chat.
2. Select **GPT-5.6 Sol / High**.
3. Send a message.
4. The first response uses **5.6 Sol**.
5. **GPT-5.6 Sol / High remains selected** afterward.

This suggests that the reliable reproduction is related to **Project chat initialization / post-first-turn state hydration**, rather than GPT-5.6 Sol / High being unavailable.

## Windows Desktop observation

A closely related behavior is also reproducible in the Windows Desktop app:

- In a Project chat, the first turn can use **5.6 Sol**, then the conversation switches toward **GPT-6 / Medium** for subsequent turns.
- In one non-Project Windows Desktop test, a newly created chat selected as **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** used **6 Thinking** from the first response.

The Web + Project reproduction above is the primary report because it is the cleanest A/B control and the per-message attribution directly demonstrates the model transition.

## Evidence

Screenshots captured by the user show:

1. A Project conversation initially configured as **GPT-5.6 Sol / High**.
2. First-response attribution showing **5.6 Sol**.
3. The reasoning selector changing to **Medium** after the first response.
4. A following response with attribution showing **6 Thinking**.
5. A non-Project Web control where **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** remains stable.

The screenshots can be attached to this issue separately.

## Possibly related issues

- #44769 — **Codex Desktop: reasoning effort resets to Medium in a new project chat until the first message**
  - Very similar Project-scoped reasoning state problem, but that report describes the reset **before** the first message.
  - In this reproduction, the first request is correctly executed with the selected model and the state changes **after the first turn**, with subsequent requests actually routed to GPT-6.
- #54618 — **Codex Windows app automatically switches manually selected model from GPT-5.6 Luna to GPT-6 Astra Light**
  - Related silent model-selection persistence failure on Windows.
- #53186 — **[Windows App] GPT-5.5 migration notice repeats after selecting GPT-6.1 Sol; High intermittently resets to Medium**
  - Related because it includes runtime evidence of High → Medium transitions, not only picker UI changes.
- #47710 — **Model selection reverts to gpt-6-astra in every new remote chat**
  - Related new-chat model reconciliation issue, although it concerns remote chats and reverts before the first message.
- #36163 — **[App] Allow the model picker to override project-scoped model defaults**
  - Related to project-scoped/default state overriding explicit picker selections.

## Why this may be distinct from #44769

#44769 reports that reasoning selections other than Medium do not stick **before the first message** in a new Project chat, and that the control works after the first message.

Here, the explicit **GPT-5.6 Sol / High** selection is successfully used for the **first request**, but after that first turn the conversation changes to **Medium**, and the next response is actually attributed to **6 Thinking**.

That makes this look like a post-first-turn Project state reconciliation/hydration problem that can alter the effective model, not only a pre-first-message reasoning picker issue.

### What variant of Codex are you using?
Codex Desktop — Composer Predictions (gray inline suggested follow-up prompts accepted with Tab).

### What feature would you like to see?
**Persist a small, per-thread history of generated Composer Predictions**, so useful suggested next steps can be recovered after they disappear, a thread is reopened, or the desktop app restarts.

Suggested UX:
- A small history/dropdown icon near the composer to view recent predictions for the current thread.
- Clicking an entry inserts it into an editable draft; **never auto-send**.

- Preserve any existing draft and respect disabled prediction settings.
- Optionally let users pin particularly useful suggestions for later.

### Why this matters
During multi-project, long-running development sessions, Composer Predictions often surface valuable next tasks, review ideas, and improvements. After returning to several conversations the next day, many previously visible predictions had disappeared. There was no way to retrieve their exact text. These are useful task ideas, not merely disposable autocomplete.

### Related requests (avoiding duplication)
- #54317 already requests **manual regeneration and alternative suggestions**; this issue deliberately does **not** re-request that button.
- #42587 concerns introducing context-aware follow-up suggestions.
- #55219 reports predictions disappearing after a desktop update, but is a reliability bug rather than a request for retained suggestion history.

**Acceptance criteria:** A previously generated but unaccepted prediction remains accessible from that thread's history after switching threads and restarting Codex, without automatically submitting or overwriting any user text.

items.title: [Feature Request] From Scrollable Chat Logs to Navigable Development Histories in Codex Desktop

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

This issue is for App and Web, actually I use all of them

### What feature would you like to see?

[Feature Request] From Scrollable Chat Logs to Navigable Development Histories in Codex Desktop

1. The Problem: Linear Scrolling Doesn’t Scale Well for Coding Agents

I think the current conversation navigation experience in the Codex desktop app could be significantly improved.

Right now, navigating a long conversation primarily relies on scrolling through its contents.

This works reasonably well for traditional chat applications, where conversations are usually short and relatively linear.

However, coding agents are fundamentally different.

A single Codex session may contain:

* Multiple implementation tasks
* Architectural discussions and decisions
* Dozens or hundreds of tool calls
* Code modifications and debugging cycles
* Failed attempts and alternative approaches
* Testing and verification steps

As these interactions accumulate, finding a specific previous discussion, implementation decision, or debugging step becomes increasingly difficult.

The problem isn’t simply that conversations are long. It’s that the current navigation model doesn’t reflect the structure of the work being performed.

I believe coding agents need a more structured way to navigate their interaction histories.

2. A Different Perspective: Development History Instead of Chat History

Rather than treating a Codex session as a linear sequence of messages, I think it would be more useful to treat it as a navigable development history.

For example, imagine a session organized like this:

📁 Implement Authentication
│
├── 💬 Discuss architecture
│
├── 🔧 Implement login API
│   ├── Read existing code
│   ├── Modify authentication logic
│   └── Run tests
│
├── 🐛 Fix authentication bug
│   ├── Investigate error
│   └── Apply fix
│
└── ✅ Final verification

Each node could be clickable, allowing users to jump directly to the corresponding position in the conversation.

This would make it much easier to understand what happened during a development session and revisit specific decisions or actions.

Importantly, this doesn’t necessarily require changing how Codex executes tasks.

It could initially be implemented as a navigation layer on top of the existing conversation interface.

3. Suggested Solution A: Clickable Conversation Navigation

The simplest improvement would be a collapsible navigation sidebar.

Instead of manually scrolling through hundreds of messages, users could navigate directly to relevant sections.

Potential features:

* Message navigation: Jump directly to any user message.
* Task navigation: Group interactions by task or implementation stage.
* Automatic headings: Generate short labels for important conversation sections.
* Tool-call grouping: Collapse repetitive tool calls and execution logs.
* Active position tracking: Highlight the current section while scrolling.
* Search integration: Search conversation content and jump directly to matching messages.

For example:

Conversation Navigation
─────────────────────────
▼ Authentication Feature
  ├─ Initial requirements
  ├─ Architecture discussion
  ├─ Implementation
  ├─ Debugging
  └─ Final verification
▼ Database Migration
  ├─ Schema discussion
  ├─ Migration implementation
  └─ Testing

Clicking any item would immediately navigate to the relevant message or section.

Even this relatively small UI improvement would make long Codex sessions much easier to use.

4. Suggested Solution B: Tree-Based Conversation Navigation

A more advanced approach would be to introduce a tree-based conversation interface.

Development workflows are rarely perfectly linear.

Developers frequently:

* Explore multiple implementation approaches.
* Return to previous architectural decisions.
* Abandon unsuccessful solutions.
* Revisit earlier debugging steps.
* Compare different implementation strategies.

A tree-based interface could represent these relationships more naturally.

For example:

Initial Requirements
        │
        ▼
Architecture Design
        │
        ├───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼
   Approach A       Approach B
        │               │
        ▼               ▼
   Implementation   Implementation
        │               │
        ▼               ▼
     Testing          Testing
        │
        ▼
   Final Solution

Users could navigate between different branches without losing track of previous work.

In the future, these branches might even be associated with Git commits, checkpoints, or implementation snapshots.

However, I don’t think full conversation branching is necessary for the initial improvement.

A hierarchical navigation view for existing conversations would already provide substantial value.

5. Why This Matters for Agent-Based Development

Traditional chat interfaces are primarily designed for exchanging messages.

Coding agents, on the other hand, perform work.

Their interaction histories contain not just conversations, but also the reasoning, actions, results, and decisions involved in completing development tasks.

As coding agents become more capable, individual sessions will likely become longer and more complex.

This creates an important UI challenge:

How can users efficiently understand, navigate, and revisit the work performed by an agent?

I believe the answer should involve more than improving scrolling.

The interface should help users understand the structure of the development process itself.

A navigable development history could make Codex more useful for:

* Reviewing previous implementation decisions
* Understanding how a bug was introduced or resolved
* Returning to specific stages of a task
* Auditing agent actions
* Continuing work after long interruptions
* Comparing alternative solutions

6. A Practical Implementation Path

I think this could be introduced incrementally.

Phase 1 — Basic Navigation

Add a collapsible sidebar listing user messages.

Clicking an item jumps to its position in the conversation.

This alone would address the most immediate usability issue.

Phase 2 — Structured Navigation

Automatically group messages and tool calls into meaningful task sections.

Introduce hierarchical navigation and collapsible sections.

Phase 3 — Development History

Explore more advanced features such as:

* Conversation branching
* Task dependency visualization
* Checkpoint navigation
* Git commit associations
* Alternative implementation comparison

These features could be developed progressively without requiring a complete redesign from the beginning.

7. Final Thoughts

I think the Codex desktop app already provides a powerful environment for agent-based development, but its conversation navigation could better reflect the complexity of modern coding workflows.

My main suggestion is simple:

Stop treating the conversation history as just a long document that users need to scroll through.

Instead, consider treating it as a structured, navigable record of the development process.

Even a lightweight clickable navigation sidebar would be a meaningful first step.

A tree-based development history could be a natural longer-term evolution.

The goal isn’t to make the interface more complicated.

It’s to make increasingly complex agent workflows easier to understand and navigate.

### Additional information

_No response_

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.163.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT sign-in

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol (low)

### What platform is your computer?

Linux 7.2.11-arch1-1 x86_64

### What issue are you seeing?

An MCP tool call started inside a code-mode `exec` script gets `item.started` but never `item.completed` when the script ends before the call returns. The turn still completes. Clients therefore show the call as in progress until they give up on it themselves.

In a T3 Code client (which uses app-server), eight such calls stayed "running" for 10 to 41 minutes each before the turn ended, although the scripts that started them had ended within 0 to 237 seconds. In each case, one of the following ended the script:

- the agent's `wait` with `terminate: true`;
- a throw in the script;
- `code-mode host exited with status exit status: 0`.

The rollout files have no `item_completed` for any of them, while the same rollouts record hundreds of normally finished `McpToolCall` items.

The MCP server is also never told: it receives no `notifications/cancelled` before it is shut down at the end of the run.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Save this stdio MCP server as `server.mjs`. It has one tool that answers after 30 s.

```js
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";
const send = (m) => process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(m) + "\n");
createInterface({ input: process.stdin }).on("line", (line) => {
  const m = JSON.parse(line);
  if (m.method === "initialize")
    send({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: m.id, result: { protocolVersion: m.params.protocolVersion, capabilities: { tools: {} }, serverInfo: { name: "slowprobe", version: "0" } } });
  else if (m.method === "tools/list")
    send({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: m.id, result: { tools: [{ name: "slow_echo", description: "Echo text back after 30 seconds.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["text"] } }] } });
  else if (m.method === "tools/call")
    setTimeout(() => send({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: m.id, result: { content: [{ type: "text", text: String(m.params.arguments?.text) }] } }), 30_000);
  else if (m.id !== undefined) send({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: m.id, result: {} });
});
```

2. Run:

```sh
codex exec --json --skip-git-repo-check -s read-only \
  -c 'mcp_servers.slowprobe.command="node"' -c 'mcp_servers.slowprobe.args=["/path/to/server.mjs"]' \
  "Run exactly one code-mode exec script that starts the slowprobe slow_echo tool with text 'hi' WITHOUT awaiting it, then waits 2 seconds (await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000))), then throws new Error('stop'). Do not retry or call slow_echo any other way. Then reply 'done'." </dev/null
```

Non-message events:

```
thread.started
turn.started
item.started   mcp_tool_call item_1 in_progress slowprobe slow_echo
turn.completed
```

As a control, the same prompt with the call awaited gives `item.started`, then `item.completed mcp_tool_call item_1 completed` 30 s later.

When the call was started with no wait before the throw, `exec --json` showed no `item.started` either. The log printed `ERROR codex_core::tools::router: error=tool call cancelled`, and the rollout had no `McpToolCall` item.

### What is the expected behavior?

When a code-mode script ends with nested tool calls still in flight, Codex should finish each started call item with a terminal status (failed or cancelled) before the turn completes. It should also send `notifications/cancelled` to the MCP server for a request it will no longer read.

### Additional information

The same pattern is probably not limited to MCP calls (any nested call a script leaves in flight), but I only tested MCP.

Assisted by: Claude (Claude Code)

If this repository cannot investigate the hosted retrieval backend, please identify the supported private escalation route or transfer/reference this report to the responsible team. We are requesting technical diagnosis, not a change to search rankings or recommendations.

## Search-result/open inconsistency

Earlier tests on October 18-20 showed updated text in search results or a linking guide while opening the target case returned an older copy or "Failed to fetch ...: Cache miss".

Example public case:
https://www.momolaw.co.kr/case/probation/sexual-exploitation-material-probation/

On 2026-10-19 around 00:14-00:16 UTC, a search result exposed updated text but following the result reference returned Cache miss. The earlier origin log recorded OAI-SearchBot receiving HTTP 200 for this case on October 18 at 13:07:56 UTC. That separate successful request does not prove that the failing request reached the origin.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

In Codex desktop, ask the built-in web tool to open these public canonical URLs and report actual document content, without browser or shell fallback:

1. https://www.momolaw.co.kr/case/probation/indecent-assault-prior-records-no-settlement-probation/

The third URL was a readable control in the previous day's comparison but failed today. These are approximate test-window timestamps, not provider-issued request timestamps.

### What is the expected behavior?

Please retrieve the current public document, or expose an actionable failure reason. Specifically, please determine:

1. Whether a live external fetch was attempted for the failing hosted requests.
2. Whether failure occurred during URL eligibility/robots handling, cache or index lookup, live fallback, network fetch, or body extraction.
3. Whether search-result and open retrieval are using inconsistent document versions or stale negative-cache records.
4. Whether the supplied feedback identifier lets the team find the failing requests; if not, what minimum additional identifier can be obtained through a supported UI.
5. Whether a site-side change is actually required, and the precise change supported by the trace.

Related symptoms have been reported in #49516 and #51196. This report adds a different public origin and search-result/open version divergence; it does not establish a shared root cause. Please link it to an existing issue if appropriate.

No credentials, cookies, account email, raw server logs, visitor IPs, private case documents, or full conversations are attached. The URLs are already public. Please request any further sensitive diagnostics through an appropriate private channel.

### Additional information

## Environment and scope

## Controls and hosting-provider response

- On October 19, the hosting provider's technical support reported no proxy/web-server rejection, rate limit, or connection-failure records in the specified October 18 failure windows or October 19 06:32-06:33 UTC comparison window. They reported ChatGPT-User and OAI-SearchBot responses of 200/301 in the October 18 web logs.
- The provider explicitly said OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User and bingbot are excluded from the rate limit applied to some training crawlers. It corrected an earlier automated answer claiming a domain-wide one-request-per-second limit.
- These are bounded historical observations and the provider's statements, not proof that every possible edge/network failure is excluded.
- Bing currently shows one reproduction URL discovered but not crawled and an older stored copy for another. We do not assume that Bing indexing delay and the Codex open failure have the same cause.
- No firewall was disabled for these comparisons.

PhpStorm 2026.2.3 integrated terminal, build PS-262.10968.76 (September 17, 2026), using the Classic terminal engine.

JetBrains Runtime 25.0.4+1-b508.27 amd64; toolkit `sun.awt.wl.WLToolkit` (native Wayland). Multiplexer usage was not recorded.

### Codex doctor report

Not collected. The observations below were confirmed interactively by the user; this report was prepared and submitted by their assistant at their request.

### What issue are you seeing?

When resuming an existing Codex CLI session inside PhpStorm, the vertical terminal scrollbar is not visible, even after switching PhpStorm's terminal engine to Classic. Restarting Codex with `--no-alt-screen` restores the expected scrollbar/scrollback behavior.

The missing scrollbar initially looked like a PhpStorm terminal regression. A newly opened Classic terminal tab displays the scrollbar, but resuming Codex without the workaround reproduces the missing-scrollbar experience.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. In PhpStorm 2026.2.3 on the environment above, select Settings > Tools > Terminal > Terminal engine > Classic.

4. Observe that the vertical terminal scrollbar is not visible.
5. Exit Codex and resume with `codex resume --no-alt-screen`.
6. Observe that the scrollbar/normal terminal scrollback behavior is restored. The user confirmed this workaround works.

### What is the expected behavior?

A resumed conversation should offer an obvious way to navigate its history with a visible scrollbar. If hiding the host terminal scrollbar is intentional in alternate-screen mode, the CLI should make the inline-mode workaround discoverable or provide an equivalent visible navigation affordance.

### Additional information

This is a user-confirmed usability/terminal compatibility report, not a confirmed rendering defect or proven Wayland-specific bug. Alternate-screen behavior may explain the disappearance; the cause has not been isolated beyond the successful `--no-alt-screen` comparison.

No claim is made about which Codex version introduced this behavior, whether it affects fresh sessions, or whether keyboard/mouse-wheel history navigation is also broken.

items.title: app-server: metadata-only pre-input state query for unmaterialized threads

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI / app-server 0.163.0 on macOS arm64 and Linux aarch64.

The same relevant error remains in main `c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415`, which was inspected but not run.

### What feature would you like to see?

Is there a supported metadata-only query for a loaded, unmaterialized thread's pre-input state, without creating a rollout solely to inspect it?

For session-peer's experimental existing-session delivery, we need to distinguish a genuine pre-input state from history that cannot currently be queried. We do not interpret an unavailable-history error or an empty preview as proof that no input has occurred. Ideally an optional enqueue precondition could check the expected state and owner atomically, covering competing input between observation and submission.

The ordinary `thread/start` then `turn/start` flow for an app-owned conversation is understood. This question concerns observing an already-loaded target; discovery and binding of an existing TUI remain separate requirements.

### Additional information

In private app-server processes with network access blocked:

1. Initialize with `capabilities.experimentalApi: true`, then send `initialized`.
2. Call `thread/start` with a private cwd and `ephemeral:false`. Test default, explicit `historyMode:"legacy"`, and explicit `historyMode:"paginated"` separately.
3. Read the returned thread with `thread/read` and `includeTurns:false`.
4. Call `thread/turns/list` with that ID, `limit:1`, and `itemsView:"notLoaded"`.

All six platform/mode cells created the thread successfully and returned empty preview metadata, then rejected the history query with code `-32600` and the classification `thread/turns/list is unavailable before first user message`.

No TUI was attached and no queue or turn submission was issued. This is a native API capability check, not evidence of TUI delivery or model receipt.

This matches the upstream [unmaterialized-thread regression](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/thread_read.rs#L1659) and [error mapping](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L6349). We avoided `thread/read(includeTurns:true)` because the paginated path can persist the thread. This does not claim that the existing history behavior is itself a bug; we are asking for a supported observation contract.

Related #43053 concerns attaching/resuming a fresh thread from another client and discusses materializing history. This request is a non-materializing state query; it does not request that resume workaround or a general history read. Empty-thread archive/resume reports such as #33120 are also adjacent but distinct.

Would an explicit readiness/materialization state or another existing API be the intended integration point? A documented guarantee and version scope would be more useful than relying on private database rows or preview text.

items.title: app-server: opt-in writer-incarnation precondition for queued input

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI / app-server. Contract review of 0.163.0 (`83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012`) and main `c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415`.

This request is based on schema/source inspection, not a live owner-race reproduction.

### What feature would you like to see?

Is there a supported way to bind queued input to the exact writer incarnation observed by a sender, and reject it if that owner is replaced before acceptance or consumption?

For session-peer, an operator may choose a currently running session and want the message to reach that particular owner. Resuming the same thread later is a different owner lifetime even when its thread ID remains unchanged.

An opt-in contract could provide:

1. An opaque incarnation minted on ownership acquisition and scoped to the thread and persistence domain.
2. An expected-incarnation check synchronized with native enqueue admission.
3. The same expectation retained with queued input and checked at dispatch, preventing a successor from consuming it merely by loading the thread.
4. A typed stale-owner outcome and documented crash/restart behavior.

The legacy thread-addressed behavior could remain unchanged when the caller does not select this mode. A client message ID alone would not imply deduplication, exactly-once delivery or permission to resend after an uncertain result.

### Additional information

The reviewed [queue-add parameters](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs#L941) contain threadId, input and clientUserMessageId. [Queue insertion](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/queued_items.rs#L79) does not expose the expected-owner predicate described here. The generated experimental schema from the installed 0.163.0 executable agrees on those fields.

Writer PID/start-time rechecks do not atomically bind a later enqueue. Session tree IDs survive resume. `turn/steer.expectedTurnId` addresses one active turn; it does not appear to supply this queued-input owner-lifetime contract.

Useful acceptance cases would include replacement before enqueue, replacement after enqueue but before dispatch, copied thread UUIDs in another store, and restart/transport uncertainty. These are requested tests, not completed experiments.

Related: #45976 and #44662 concern attribution/receipts and broader delivery; #42591 requests signed invocation identity. This request is specifically an enforced queue precondition across ownership lifetimes, not a new cryptographic attestation service or reply-reading interface.

If an existing contract covers this already, please point us to its supported version and owner-replacement semantics.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI / app-server 0.163.0, macOS arm64 and Linux aarch64.

Source comparison: rust-v0.163.0 (`83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012`) and main `c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415`. Main was inspected, not executed.

### What feature would you like to see?

Is there a supported API for identifying the actual persistence domain used by a running app-server, distinct from its account home and reloaded configuration? If not, please consider exposing an opaque live-storage identity and an optional expected-storage precondition checked atomically when admitting queued input.

I maintain session-peer, which discovers existing sessions and forwards messages. The use case is checking that metadata discovery and submission refer to the same store. Matching a thread UUID or account home cannot establish that when different stores may contain copies of the same thread.

The intended API would distinguish server/store replacement and define what happens after restart or a database copy. A path alone would not provide this identity. This is a capability/contract question, not a report of demonstrated misdelivery or an exploit.

### Additional information

Credential-free, initialization-only probes on both platforms observed:

| Private test configuration | Server's open state DB | `config/read` SQLite field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No override | Account home | null/absent |
| Environment only | Environment-selected directory | null/absent |
| User config plus environment | User-config directory | User-config directory |
| CLI override plus user config/environment | CLI-selected directory | CLI-selected directory |
| Change private config A to B while server runs | Remains A | Changes to B |
| Restart after that change | B | Not needed for this control |

Minimal A/B procedure: start `codex app-server --listen stdio://` with a fresh HOME/CODEX_HOME and user config selecting private SQLite directory A; initialize; inspect that process's open state DB handles; change only the private config to B; call `config/read` again; compare the handles; finally restart as a control.

All initialized servers reported the expected `codexHome` for their case.

The probes blocked network access and issued no thread, queue or model-turn requests. Host system configuration was absent; macOS forced preferences were absent. Windows, actual MDM policies and managed-daemon routing were not tested. Process file handles were laboratory evidence, not a proposed production API.

Source context:

- [Queue store retains startup state](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/app-server/src/message_processor.rs#L308).
- [Config reads reload layers](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c7234c1174b27d9c55199fba0d546dc27d1b0415/codex-rs/app-server/src/config_manager_service.rs#L119).
- #55300 adds startup requirements discovery without initializing storage; this request concerns the store already held by a running process.
- #52050 concerns shared history across hosts; this request is narrower and does not request cross-node storage support.

If an existing versioned API already covers this use case, a reference would help us avoid duplicating it.

items.title: [macOS][Chrome] Claimed existing tab returns extension UI guard after successful connection

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

On macOS, the Chrome browser-use provider discovers an existing tab and `user.claimTab` succeeds, but `Tab.playwright.domSnapshot` then returns:

> Google Chrome is blocking automation because another extension UI is open on this page. Complete or dismiss that extension UI in Google Chrome, then ask me to continue.

No extension popup was visible at the time. The source of the guard is unknown; I cannot tell whether it comes from Chrome, another extension, or the browser-use bridge.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use an existing tab in the intended, signed-in Chrome profile.
2. Discover the tab through the public browser-use inventory and claim it. The claim succeeds and returns a Tab.
3. Call `Tab.playwright.domSnapshot` on that Tab. The guard above is returned.
4. Reset the public REPL once, bootstrap a fresh provider, claim the same existing tab again, and call the same method. The same guard is returned.

In a separate investigation, a self-created tab in the same Chrome profile accepted four `playwright.domSnapshot` calls. This does not establish that every new tab works; the tool/runtime, tab provenance, and timing differed. A prior normal Chrome restart also did not restore this existing-tab workflow.

### What is the expected behavior?

After a successful claim, DOM access should work in the selected tab. If an extension UI must be dismissed, the error should identify a supported way to determine which UI and tab/frame is blocking access, without requiring private APIs or bypassing the guard.

### Additional information

- Main affected Codex chat ID: `01a14473-5c79-7412-a601-b002a6a43583`.
- Feedback was recorded separately with no logs: `01a15cc8-27cd-7540-9234-3ce648c97d34`.
- There is no confirmed lower-level error code or trace connecting the guard text to its originating process.
- The earlier multiple-profile report #31540 may be related, but the target profile was verified for this observation. This report concerns the guard after a successful tab claim.
- No site content, credentials, email addresses, screenshots, or raw session logs are included.

Is there a public diagnostic for the originating error and extension UI owner, and a supported recovery procedure when this guard persists after claim and a standard REPL reset?
